498.title: Vishvamitra takes the boys
498.hook: a king promises a visitor anything, then hears what he wants
498.howItsDone: Vishvamitra is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the great rishis; the Gayatri mantra of the Rig Veda is traditionally credited to him, and his request for Rama is told as the moment the prince's life of service begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice, part three. Ravana scorned humans, and four sons were born. Did you let one overlooked thing count? Now the boys have grown. Day four hundred ninety-eight.
screen: `FOUR SONS, BORN TO ANSWER A BOAST.`

segments.voice: The four princes grow up learned, brave and close. Lakshmana sticks to Rama like a second shadow; Shatrughna to Bharata. Dasharatha, delighted, is already talking with his counselors about their weddings. Then a guard rushes in: the sage Vishvamitra is at the gate. Dasharatha hurries out to meet him, washes his feet, honors him, and says the words a king says to an honored guest, and maybe shouldn't: whatever you ask, consider it done. Vishvamitra smiles, and asks.
screen: `FOUR PRINCES, GROWN.` → `A FAMOUS SAGE AT THE GATE.` → `WHATEVER YOU ASK, IT'S DONE.`

segments.voice: Vishvamitra explains. He's begun a sacrifice, and two rakshasas, Maricha and Subahu, keep wrecking it, pouring blood and flesh on the altar. Under his vow he can't curse them in anger. So he asks for Rama. Give me your eldest son, the boy who still wears a child's side-locks, for ten nights, to guard my rite. And Dasharatha's world tilts. He nearly faints. Then he pleads, and Valmiki gives us his words: unashodasha-varsho me ramo rajivalochanah. My lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen. He's never fought. Take my army instead. Take me. I'll fight them myself. And then, when he hears who stands behind Maricha and Subahu, he grows more frightened still: Ravana. No, not Rama. Now, who is Vishvamitra? He wasn't born a sage. He was born a king, a warrior who, the Ramayana tells later, spent ages of fierce austerity until he became a brahmarshi, a sage of the highest rank. His name means friend of the whole world. And he's famous for his fire. When Dasharatha takes back his promise, that fire rises. The sage says: you're breaking your word, king. Fine. I'll go as I came. And the whole earth, the text says, trembles. Under the noise of the scene is something quiet. A father who has promised his son away, and can't bear to let him go.
screen: `TWO RAKSHASAS RUIN HIS SACRIFICE.` · `RAMA IS NOT YET SIXTEEN.` · `A KING WHO BECAME A SAGE.` · `A PROMISE TAKEN BACK.` · then, large: `ŪNAṢOḌAŚAVARṢO ME RĀMO RĀJĪVALOCANAḤ.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone you love who is stepping into something bigger than you'd like: a child, a friend, a younger sibling, maybe your younger self. Notice if part of you wants to hold on. Don't argue with it. Then, on each breath out, loosen your grip by one finger. Not letting them go, just loosening. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Vishvamitra, friend of the whole world. The king-turned-sage asks Dasharatha for Rama to guard his sacrifice, and a father's promise meets a father's fear.
Your line: Rama is not yet sixteen. Today, before you say whatever you want, it's yours, pause for one breath and ask what it might cost. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 498 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VISHVAMITRA TAKES THE BOYS, PART TWO.`

499.title: Vishvamitra takes the boys
499.hook: the verse that wakes Rama on his first morning away from home is still sung at dawn
499.howItsDone: The Venkatesha Suprabhatam, sung at dawn at the Tirumala temple and played in many homes, opens with Vishvamitra's verse from the Bala Kanda waking Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra takes the boys, part one. A promise, a plea, and a sage's anger shaking the earth. Did you pause before promising whatever someone wanted? Today, the boys go. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

In many homes and temples in South India, the day starts with a recording of a Sanskrit hymn called the Venkatesha Suprabhatam, a song to wake the Lord at Tirupati. Its very first verse isn't new. It's borrowed, word for word, from the Ramayana. It's what Vishvamitra says to wake Rama on his first morning away from home, sleeping on grass by a river. Before we get there, though, the boys have to leave.
screen: `A HYMN AT DAWN IN SOUTH INDIA.` → `ITS FIRST VERSE IS FROM THE RAMAYANA.` → `RAMA'S FIRST MORNING AWAY.`

segments.voice: Vasishtha, the royal priest, speaks to the frightened king. You've given your word, he says. Breaking it would undo all your merit. And look who's asking. Vishvamitra knows every divine weapon there is. Rama will be safer with him than anywhere. Dasharatha listens, and yields. He calls for Rama, and Lakshmana, who won't be left behind, and blesses them. The boys walk out after the sage, bows in hand, quivers on their backs, and the text says a soft breeze blew and flowers fell from the sky. After a day's walk, on the south bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra stops and teaches Rama two mantras, bala and atibala, strength and great strength. With these, he says, you won't feel hunger or thirst or tiredness, and no one will match you, awake or asleep. That night, the princes sleep on grass, like ordinary travelers. And at dawn, the sage wakes them: kausalya supraja rama purva sandhya pravartate, uttishtha narashardula kartavyam daivam ahnikam. Rama, fortunate son of Kausalya, the morning twilight is here. Rise, tiger among men, the day's sacred duties are waiting. The boys rise, bathe, say their prayers, and walk on, to a hermitage where, the sage tells them, Shiva once burned Kama, the god of desire, to ash. The boys have left their father's house. Their teacher's world has begun.
screen: `VASISHTHA: KEEP YOUR WORD.` · `THE BOYS WALK OUT, FLOWERS FALL.` · `BALA AND ATIBALA BY THE RIVER.` · `A SAGE WAKES THEM AT DAWN.` · then, large: `KAUSALYĀ SUPRAJĀ RĀMA PŪRVĀ SANDHYĀ PRAVARTATE.`

segments.voice: Sit as if it's very early, the light just starting. Let the breath be slow, like someone waking. Imagine a kind voice saying your name, the way Vishvamitra said Rama's: not rushing you, just letting you know the day has come. On each breath in, rise a little. On each breath out, settle into the day you actually have. The bell holds the time.
Atibala, great strength, one of the two mantras Vishvamitra teaches Rama. Persuaded by Vasishtha, Dasharatha lets Rama and Lakshmana go, and the sage teaches them, and wakes them, on the road.
Your line: rise, tiger among men. Tomorrow morning, wake someone, or yourself, the way the sage did: by name, gently, with the day's good work waiting. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 21–22 (Vasishtha's counsel; departure; bala and atibala)

500.title: Tataka
500.hook: a forest that used to be farmland, and the story of who emptied it
500.howItsDone: Tataka's story is told in Ramayana recitations and in Ramlila performances as the young Rama's first test; some teachers pause on Rama's question and Vishvamitra's answer as a lesson about the duty to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra takes the boys, part two. Bala and atibala, and a sage waking Rama at dawn. Did you wake someone gently? And notice the number today. Five hundred days. Day five hundred.

The three travelers cross the Ganga where the Sarayu pours into it, and Rama hears the roar of the two rivers meeting. On the far side, the land changes. A dark, thick forest. No paths. Crickets, harsh birdcalls, lions, tigers, boars, elephants. Nobody lives here. Rama asks what anyone would ask: what is this place? And Vishvamitra tells him something surprising. This wasn't always a forest. Not long ago, these were two rich farming lands, full of people and harvests. Someone emptied them.
screen: `WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` → `A FOREST WITH NO PATHS.` → `IT USED TO BE FARMLAND.`

segments.voice: Her name is Tataka. The sage tells her story. She was born a yakshi, a nature spirit, daughter of a yaksha named Suketu, who had prayed for a child and was given a daughter with the strength of a thousand elephants. She married Sunda, and had a son, Maricha. Remember that name; we met him two days ago, ruining Vishvamitra's sacrifice. When her husband died, Tataka and her son attacked the great sage Agastya, and Agastya cursed them both. Maricha became a rakshasa. And Tataka lost her beauty and became a terrible devourer. Since then, she has turned this whole country into wilderness. And now the sage says: for the good of the land and everyone who should be living here, she has to be stopped. By you. Rama stops. Valmiki lets him ask a real question, and it matters that he does. She's a woman. How can a woman have such strength? And the sage, knowing what Rama is really asking, makes his case before Rama acts. Rulers, he says, have a duty to protect. When anyone, man or woman, is destroying the lives of others, the protector cannot step back. He gives examples from the old stories, where even the gods acted against women who meant the world harm. It's a hard teaching, and the text doesn't hide that it's hard. A young prince, outside the walls for the first time, is being asked to do something that goes against his upbringing. Tomorrow, what he decides.
screen: `FARMLAND TURNED TO WILDERNESS.` · `A YAKSHI, CURSED BY AGASTYA.` · `RAMA STOPS AND ASKS.` · `THE PROTECTOR CANNOT STEP BACK.` · then, large: `TĀṬAKĀ.`

segments.voice: Five hundred days. Sit with that for a moment. Then picture a place that was once full of life and went quiet: a closed shop, an empty field, a friendship that went dry. Breathe toward it. Not to fix it right now. Just to remember what it was, and to hold the hope that what's empty can be lived in again. Let the breath be steady and slow. The bell holds the time.
Tataka. The yakshi, cursed by Agastya, who turned two rich lands into wilderness, and whom Vishvamitra asks Rama to stop.
Your line: Rama stops and asks. Today, when you're asked to do something hard, let yourself ask your real question first, out loud, the way Rama did. Day five hundred.

screen: `DAY 500 COUNTS.` → `FIVE HUNDRED DAYS.` → `TOMORROW: TATAKA, PART TWO.`

501.title: Tataka
501.hook: Rama decides, and tries the gentlest way first
501.howItsDone: In Ramayana recitation and performance, Tataka's defeat is told as Rama's first act of protecting the land; commentators and modern readers discuss it in different ways, and some draw attention to Rama's reluctance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tataka, part one. A forest that used to be farmland, a yakshi under a curse, and Rama stopping to ask his real question. Did you ask yours before doing something hard? Day five hundred one.

Rama has listened. Now he answers, and his answer is worth hearing, because it isn't simply yes. He says: my father told me to do whatever you say. So I'll do this, for the sake of the cows, the sages and the land. He's acting from obedience, from a promise, not from appetite for a fight. Then he lifts his bow and twangs the string. The sound rolls through the forest. And from somewhere deep in the trees, something hears it and comes running.
screen: `MY FATHER TOLD ME TO OBEY YOU.` → `THE TWANG OF THE BOWSTRING.` → `SOMETHING COMES RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Tataka charges out, raising clouds of dust, hurling rocks. Slow down here, because Valmiki does. Rama doesn't try to kill her. He says to Lakshmana: I'll just take away her power to harm. I don't want to take her life. He shoots and cuts off her arms. Lakshmana wounds her face. That should end it. It doesn't. Tataka uses her magic, turns invisible, changes shape, and rains stones on them from the air. Vishvamitra calls out: enough mercy, Rama. Evening is coming, and at dusk rakshasas grow stronger. And so Rama, tracking her by sound, looses an arrow, and Tataka falls. The gods appear and praise Rama, and Vishvamitra embraces him and kisses his head. And the forest, the text says, is freed, and becomes beautiful again. How do people read this scene? Traditional teachers see Rama's first act of protection, a land given back to the people meant to live in it, and they point to how hard he tried not to kill. Some modern readers find it painful, a young man pressed to kill a woman, and they read the story with that discomfort in view. Both readings take the text seriously. What the text itself makes plain is the order of things. He asked first. He obeyed a promise. He tried to disarm before he destroyed. And only when that failed, he finished it.
screen: `HE TRIES TO DISARM, NOT KILL.` · `SHE TURNS INVISIBLE, RAINS STONES.` · `AT DUSK, THE FINAL ARROW.` · `TWO WAYS PEOPLE READ IT.` · then, large: `THE FOREST IS FREED.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of a situation where you had to be firm with someone, or will have to. Before anything else, ask: what's the gentlest thing that would actually work? Hold that question with the breath. Don't plan the whole conversation. Just let the gentlest effective step come into view, and rest with it. The bell holds the time.
Tataka. Rama, obeying his father's word, first tries to disarm her, and only when her magic goes on does he loose the arrow that frees the forest.
Your line: disarm before he destroyed. Today, when you need to stop something, try the gentlest step that would actually work before you reach for anything stronger. Day five hundred one.

502.title: the weapons
502.hook: the morning after the forest is freed, the sage hands over everything he has
502.howItsDone: In the epics, astras are given by teachers or gods to those judged worthy, invoked by mantra; Hindu storytellers often use the gift to Rama to teach that power should follow character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tataka, part two. Rama obeyed a promise, tried to disarm before he destroyed, and the forest was freed. Did you try the gentlest step that would work? Day five hundred two.

They spend the night in the freed forest. In the morning, Vishvamitra is smiling. He has been watching this boy. He's seen him ask before acting, obey without sulking, try mercy before force. And now the sage does something extraordinary. He decides to hand over everything he has. Not land, not gold. Something no treasury holds, and no army could take from him. He tells Rama to sit down and get ready.
screen: `THE SAGE HAS BEEN WATCHING.` → `MERCY BEFORE FORCE.` → `NOW, EVERYTHING HE HAS.`

segments.voice: What Vishvamitra gives are the astras, the divine weapons. An astra isn't just an arrow. It's a power called up by a mantra and released through a weapon: the force of a god, carried on a word. The sage names them one after another, and the list goes on for verses. The discus of dharma and the discus of time. Indra's thunderbolt. Shiva's trident. The weapon of Brahma himself. The noose of Varuna, lord of the waters. The fire weapon, the wind weapon, and one called manava, named for Manu, the first human. As Vishvamitra recites, something strange happens. The weapons appear. Not as metal, but as beings, shining, with bodies of their own, standing before Rama with their palms joined. They say: we are yours. Tell us what to do. And Rama, still a young man, touches each one with his hand and answers simply: stay in my mind, and come when I need you. Notice what the text is saying. The weapons aren't things. They're servants with their own presence, and they bow to a person, not just a skill. And notice when they're given. Not on day one. After a test. After the sage has seen how this young man uses force when force is put in his hands. In the Ramayana, power follows character. It doesn't come first.
screen: `AN ASTRA: A GOD'S POWER ON A WORD.` · `DISCUS, THUNDERBOLT, TRIDENT, NOOSE.` · `THE WEAPONS APPEAR, PALMS JOINED.` · `POWER FOLLOWS CHARACTER.` · then, large: `STAY IN MY MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of one strength you have: a skill, a voice people listen to, money, patience, quickness with words. Picture it standing in front of you, palms joined, waiting. Don't send it anywhere yet. Just ask it, the way Rama did, to stay in your mind and come when it's truly needed. Breathe with that, a strength held in reserve. The bell holds the time.
The weapons. The astras, divine powers Vishvamitra gives Rama after Tataka, which appear as shining beings and wait on his mind.
Your line: stay in my mind. Today, hold back one strength you'd normally use, a sharp reply, a winning argument, and keep it in your mind for when it's really needed. Day five hundred two.

503.title: the weapons
503.hook: a teenager with the gods' weapons asks the one question that matters next
503.carry: teach me to call them back
503.howItsDone: Traditional teachers often point to Rama's request for the withdrawals of the weapons as a sign of his character: a wise person learns how to stop a power before using it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the weapons, part one. Divine powers, standing as shining beings, told by Rama to stay in his mind. Did you hold back one strength today? Day five hundred three.

Hand someone the keys to something enormous and listen to what they ask first. A new driver with a fast car. A new manager with the power to fire people. An eighteen-year-old with a credit card. The question is nearly always: what can this do? How fast, how far, how much? Rama has just been handed the weapons of the gods. And as they walk on through the forest, he turns to Vishvamitra with a different question. Not how do I use these. Something quieter, and wiser.
screen: `THE KEYS TO SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THE USUAL QUESTION: WHAT CAN IT DO?` → `RAMA ASKS ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: Rama says: I've received the weapons, and even the gods would find them hard to overcome. Now teach me how to call them back. In Sanskrit, the release is prayoga, and the withdrawal is samhara. Vishvamitra is delighted, and he teaches him. And again, the text says, the powers appear, a whole new company of shining beings, with names of their own, standing before Rama with palms joined. These are the withdrawals: the knowledge of how to stop what you've started. Rama asks them, too, to come to his mind when he needs them. Why would Valmiki give this a whole moment? Because in the epics, a weapon you can't call back is a disaster. Later in the epics there are stories of warriors who could launch a terrible power and not withdraw it. Rama's first instinct, this young, is to ask for the brake before he ever touches the accelerator. That's the kind of person the sage has been looking for. The road goes on, and soon they see a hermitage on a hill, green and peaceful, with deer grazing and birds calling. Rama asks whose it is. Vishvamitra says: this is Siddhashrama. Long ago, Vishnu did his austerities here, and this was the hermitage of Vamana, the dwarf, who asked King Bali for three steps of land and crossed the worlds in three strides. This is where my sacrifice is waiting. And this is where the weapons will be needed.
screen: `TEACH ME TO CALL THEM BACK.` · `PRAYOGA AND SAMHARA.` · `THE BRAKE BEFORE THE ACCELERATOR.` · `SIDDHASHRAMA, WHERE VAMANA LIVED.` · then, large: `SAṂHĀRA: THE WITHDRAWAL.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Breathe in, and notice how you start a breath. Breathe out, and notice how you let it go. Every breath has both: a release and a return. Now think of one thing you started today, a mood, a comment, a task, and practice calling it back, gently, the way you'd let a breath come home. The bell holds the time.
The weapons. Rama asks not only how to release them but how to withdraw them, and Vishvamitra teaches him the samhara, the calling back.
Your line: teach me to call them back. Today, before you start something you can't easily stop, a message, an argument, a purchase, ask yourself how you'd call it back. Day five hundred three.

504.title: the weapons
504.hook: six nights awake, a silent sage, and an arrow that chooses not to kill
504.carry: a way to walk off whole
504.howItsDone: Ramayana tellings mark Maricha's survival here because he returns in the Aranya Kanda as the golden deer; teachers often point out that Rama chose a weapon that would stun, not kill.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the weapons, part two. Rama asked how to call them back, and the sage taught him the withdrawal. Did you think about how to call something back before you started it? Today the week closes. Day five hundred four.

At Siddhashrama, Vishvamitra begins his sacrifice and takes a vow of silence. From now on, he can't say a word. So the hermits tell the boys: for six days and six nights, you have to guard him. Rama and Lakshmana stand watch, bows ready, and don't sleep. Five days pass. Nothing. On the sixth, the altar fire suddenly flares up on its own. The sky goes dark. And out of the dark comes a roar, and a rain of blood.
screen: `A VOW OF SILENCE.` → `SIX NIGHTS ON WATCH.` → `THE SIXTH DAY: A RAIN OF BLOOD.`

segments.voice: Maricha and Subahu have come, with their followers, to wreck the rite. Rama sees them and says to Lakshmana: watch this. He picks up the manava weapon, the one named for Manu, the first human, and fires it at Maricha's chest. It doesn't kill him. It lifts him and hurls him a hundred yojanas, far out over the sea, where he falls, stunned, but alive. And Rama says it plainly: the manava has knocked him senseless, but it hasn't taken his life. Then the fire weapon for Subahu, who falls dead. Then the wind weapon scatters the rest. The sacrifice is finished. Vishvamitra, his vow complete, turns to Rama and says: you've made the name of this place come true. Siddhashrama, the hermitage of accomplishment. Hold onto Maricha. He's still out there, alive, and he will come back in this story wearing a very different shape. Now the week, from the top. A father's plea that his son isn't yet sixteen. Vasishtha's counsel and the sage's dawn verse. A forest that used to be farmland. Rama asking first, and disarming before destroying. The weapons appearing with joined palms. The question of how to call them back. And today, the first real use: one enemy spared, and a promise kept.
screen: `THE MANAVA FOR MARICHA.` · `HURLED OVER THE SEA, STILL ALIVE.` · `THE FIRE WEAPON FOR SUBAHU.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `SIDDHASHRAMA: ACCOMPLISHED.`

segments.voice: Sit as if you're on watch. Not tense. Just awake. Let your eyes rest low, your back long, your breath even. Notice the sounds around you, each one arriving and passing, the way the boys watched the dark for six nights. If your attention wanders, come back to the watch without scolding yourself. Steady, alert, and calm. The bell holds the time.
The weapons. At Siddhashrama, Rama uses them for the first time: the manava hurls Maricha out to sea alive, and the sacrifice is completed.
Your line: a way to walk off whole. Today, when you win a small conflict, leave the other person a way to walk off whole. Day five hundred four.

screen: `DAY 504 COUNTS.` → `A WEEK ON THE ROAD WITH THE SAGE, DONE.` → `TOMORROW: AHALYA RESTORED.`

myth: Rama kills Maricha at Siddhashrama
the manava hurls him far over the sea, stunned but alive.
Vishvamitra keeps silent during the sacrifice
he's under a vow, so the boys stand guard for six days and nights.
Siddhashrama means something like the hermitage of accomplishment
and Vishvamitra says Rama has made the name come true.

fork.setup: you're Rama. Maricha attacks the sacrifice. you hold the manava weapon. what do you do?
options: strike him so he's hurled far away, alive.
fork.reveal: the manava hurls Maricha a hundred yojanas over the sea, senseless but alive. he'll be back, as the golden deer.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first battle is all about killing demons.
what it means: Rama chooses which weapon for whom, and spares Maricha.
what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 30 has the manava, agneya and vayavya; Maricha's survival sets up his return as the golden deer in the Aranya Kanda.
